newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE cocoa surrenders most gains at close.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE cocoa surrenders most gains at close.

text.p: London cocoa futures managed to pull themselves together after recent lows but Friday's fragile rally encountered selling and quickly ran out of steam.

U.S. fourth quarter grindings rose a sharp 10.73 percent to 95,352 tonnes but the change -- which on paper appeared to be significantly above market expectations -- reflected a downward revision in the fourth quarter total grind for 1995.
Traders said the data effectively stripped the market of another potentially bullish piece of news.
"If you take the revision into account, the net change is only one percent, which is within market expectations," said one.
But U.S. traders called the grind outcome neutral to slightly positive.
Friday's performance confirmed the market's reluctance to jolt out of its lethargic mood, at least in the short term.
A bout of selling in New York following an initial wave of speculative buying weighed on the London market in the afternoon just as March lost upside momentum above the 881-stg high.
March closed two stg higher on the day at 878 stg a tonne after trading in a range between 874 and 881 stg. Other contracts gained between two and four stg.
Turnover totalled an unimpressive 4,092 lots including some crosses on Sept and March as well as AAs. March/May was steady at 21 stg.
Traders said March was likely to remain stuck in a tight range between 876 and 890 stg for a while before manoeuvres around the position's hefty open interest provide new direction.
They cited arbitrage selling on forwards contracts and light volumes of physical offtake in the nearbys on Friday.
Technically, March needs to overcome barriers at 890 and 900 stg to appeal to holders of short positions and extend gains.
Until then the contract low of 865 stg remains vulnerable, analysts said.

"The downtrend is slowing now and it is likely we have seen the worst of the falls. But there are no signs of any serious attempt at recover yet," said Elli Gifford of Investment Research of Cambridge in her weekly technical summary.
Arrival figures from West Africa next week may provide fresh hints about the size of the crop and a possible deficit this season but a clear picture may not emerge until February.
